analysis.one_liner: Stops new production of the B-2 stealth bomber after fiscal 1990.
analysis.headline: The bill to end new B-2 bomber production drew 150 bipartisan cosponsors but never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred the Pentagon from using any money appropriated after fiscal 1990 to start building more B-2 stealth bombers, one of the most expensive aircraft in history. It would have let work continue only on bombers already in production and on research and flight testing, and it required the Defense Secretary to keep the factory tools and facilities intact so production could restart later. In practice it was a cost-control measure aimed at capping a multibillion-dollar weapons program.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, who would have been spared the cost of building additional B-2 bombers, each of which cost roughly $2 billion. Money not spent on the program could have gone to other defense priorities or deficit reduction.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits funds appropriated to the Department of Defense after fiscal 1990 from being used to commence production of any B-2 aircraft [S2] [S3].
Limits spending on the B-2 program to finishing bombers already in production and to research, development, test and evaluation, including flight testing [S2] [S3].
Requires the Secretary of Defense to preserve production facilities and tooling so the option to build the aircraft later is retained, softening the economic hit to the production base [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The B-2's contractors and their suppliers, principally the prime contractor Northrop and the bomber's subcontractor base, would lose future production revenue. Members of Congress whose districts and states had B-2 contracts would also lose the associated jobs and spending.

drawbacks.text: Terminating production would have cost jobs at B-2 contractors and their suppliers; the bill partially offset this by ordering facilities and tooling preserved for a future production option [S3].

Supporters of the bomber argued a stealth fleet was needed to counter Soviet air defenses and that stopping at a small number would raise the already enormous per-aircraft cost by eliminating the savings of a long production run — the bill keeps research and testing funded but leaves the fleet's final size to other decisions [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings from halting additional production would have been very large relative to the costs, which the bill tried to soften by preserving the production line and allowing testing to continue. The main genuine cost was to contractor communities and the loss of scale economies in the bomber program, a cost the bill acknowledged but did not fully eliminate.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Armed Services Committee and its Research and Development Subcommittee, and with the committee never acting, the bill died when this Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ronald Dellums and a bipartisan group of 25 original members introduced the bill on February 7, 1990 [S3].
The same day it was introduced, it was referred to the House Committee on Armed Services [S1] [S5].
On February 20, 1990, the Pentagon was asked for an executive comment and the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Research and Development [S5].
The bill gathered 150 cosponsors — 127 Democrats and 23 Republicans — but no further action was taken before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The B-2 contractors and the bomber program itself came out ahead: with the bill stalled in committee, new production funding faced no restriction from this bill, and the weapons program continued to draw from the defense budget.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: B-2 contractors and the bomber program

for.name: Rep. Ronald V. Dellums
for.what_they_did: Introduced the B-2 Production Termination Act on February 7, 1990.

for.name: 127 of 257 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill to end new B-2 production.

for.name: 23 of 175 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; original cosponsors included Reps. Kasich, Kolbe, Ridge, Porter, and Ireland.

against.name: House Armed Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral without holding a markup or vote; the bill never left the committee.

against.name: Subcommittee on Research and Development
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on February 20, 1990, and took no further action.

against.name: Defense aerospace industry
against.role: B-2 prime contractor and supplier network (Northrop and subcontractors)
against.what_they_did: Fought continuation of the B-2 program, which supplied billions in annual revenue and jobs concentrated in contractors' districts.

sides.party_line_note: Support crossed party lines: 127 of 257 House Democrats and 23 of 175 House Republicans cosponsored, and the original sponsors included prominent Republicans such as John Kasich, Jim Kolbe, and Tom Ridge.

industries.industry: Defense contractors (B-2 prime contractor and bomber suppliers)
industries.note: The bill would have cut off new B-2 production orders, ending a stream of multibillion-dollar contracts and the jobs attached to them. The contractors' interest in continuing production ran against taxpayers' interest in stopping an extremely expensive program.
